html:
On 9 September 1888 the Chilean naval officer Policarpo Toro signed an agreement with Rapa Nui chiefs that made the island part of Chile. The Rapa Nui text speaks of friendship; the Spanish one of cession.

The island had been ravaged by the slave raids and disease. After annexation, Chile leased most of it to a sheep company, and islanders were confined to the village of Hanga Roa until the 1960s.

Rapa Nui people won Chilean citizenship in 1966. They still press for control of their land and of the moai sites, and their language and identity have revived, helped by links with Tahiti and other Polynesian islands.
